query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, adherent, oxidation‐resistant surface coating based on Al2O3 (or an Al2O3/Cr2O3 composite) on as‐cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will inhibit oxygen ingress during high‐temperature air exposure, thereby mitigating pesting while preserving its intrinsic room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy in its as-cast condition exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength in the range of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Application of a thin, uniform oxidation‐resistant surface coating (via PVD or pack processing) containing Al2O3 or an Al2O3/Cr2O3 composite.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at approximately 800 °C for 5 hours under tensile loading at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹; mechanical performance measurements at room temperature and at 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The interface between the applied coating and the underlying alloy acts as a barrier, limiting oxygen diffusion and stabilizing the surface from rapid oxide scale spallation (pesting).
generation.mechanism: The oxidation‐resistant coating forms a dense, adherent oxide layer that effectively minimizes oxygen ingress; this protection prevents the formation and detachment of non-protective oxides on the bulk alloy while leaving the microstructure—and thus its favorable mechanical properties—unchanged.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated material, the coated alloy is predicted to exhibit significantly improved oxidation resistance (i.e., reduced mass gain and pesting during 5 h air exposure at 800 °C) while retaining the original balance of room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr shows marked oxygen-induced degradation (pesting) under the defined high-temperature conditions, which compromises its utility for practical high-temperature applications.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable within the defined temperature (approximately 800 °C), exposure duration (5 hours), atmospheric (air), and tensile loading conditions (strain rates of 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹) used in previous studies on related alloys.
generation.uncertainty: The exact thickness and composition parameters of the coating needed for optimal performance and its long-term durability under cyclic thermal or mechanical loads remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr specimens: one group with the applied thin oxidation‐resistant coating and one uncoated control group. Expose both groups to air at 800 °C for 5 hours while subjecting them to tensile loading at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹. After exposure, perform weight gain measurements, microstructural analysis (e.g., oxide layer continuity and thickness via SEM/EDS), and mechanical testing (room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature yield strength measurements).
measurements: Continuity and integrity of the oxide layer (via microscopic analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens exhibit comparable levels of oxidation (evidenced by similar mass gain and oxide layer degradation/pesting) or show a significant deterioration in room-temperature ductility and/or high-temperature yield strength relative to the uncoated controls, then the hypothesis that the coating preserves mechanical properties while improving oxygen resistance is falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. decision.trend: Over the past several years, researchers working on refractory high‐entropy alloys have explored single‐intervention strategies that preserve the inherent mechanical balance while targeting secondary challenges. In some studies the approach was to modify the alloy composition (by minor additions such as Cr, which, for example, in PMC10759803 subtly altered phases and improved overall performance without drastically undermining ductility), while in others the focus was on processing routes that induce second‐phase or composite microstructures (as in PMC7513042, where in situ ceramic reinforcements contributed to oxidation resistance and strength). However, when it comes to oxygen protection especially for these complex, high-temperature alloys, the method used in the related non‐equiatomic alloy (and hinted at in earlier oxidation‐protection work) has not been directly translated to the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; alloy modifications sometimes risk upsetting the delicate balance between room‐temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
decision.unsolved: The challenge remains to impart improved oxygen resistance (e.g., prevention of pesting during exposures around 800 °C for several hours in air) onto the equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy without altering its microstructure in a way that would compromise its established mechanical performance. While prior studies on similar systems have achieved oxidation protection through either compositional tailoring or the formation of reinforcing oxide phases, none have shown that the equiatomic composition can be similarly protected without degradation of intrinsic ductility or strength.
decision.lever: Apply a thin, adherent, oxidation‐resistant surface coating (e.g., a PVD-deposited or pack-processed scale forming layer such as Al2O3 or mixed Al2O3/Cr2O3) on as-cast HfNbTaTiZr
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of using a single external intervention to protect the alloy while leaving the bulk microstructure—and thus its favorable mechanical characteristics—unchanged. It builds on the successful oxidation‐protection strategy seen in related, non‐equiatomic alloys and in refractory systems where interfacial engineering (rather than bulk composition change) was used to prevent pesting, ensuring that performance targets (8–16% room‐temperature ductility and high yield strength at 1000 °C) are maintained. A controlled experiment could involve treating as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with the coating, exposing specimens to air at 800 °C for 5 hours at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹, and comparing the onset of oxidation and mechanical property retention against untreated samples. Failure of the hypothesis would be indicated if the coated alloy still exhibits significant pesting or if the coating adversely changes the mechanical performance.
